hook: How someone talks about people who aren't in the room tells you more about them than anything they say directly to your face
topic: How people narrate others — the signal in third-party stories
body:
**How someone talks about people who aren't in the room is one of the most information-dense signals available to you — and almost nobody knows how to read it.**

When someone tells you about a difficult relationship from their past — an ex, a friend who let them down, a colleague who was impossible to work with — listen to the structure of the story. Not just what happened. How they tell it.

Notice: are they the only coherent person in every story? Does everyone who ever hurt them get described as simply bad, crazy, or jealous — without any texture, without any sense of their own role in what unfolded?

Notice: do they ever take any responsibility — even small, partial, human responsibility — for a relationship that went wrong? Or does accountability always land somewhere else?

And notice something else: the level of contempt. Someone can talk about a person who genuinely hurt them with hurt, with sadness, with frustration — all of that is real and understandable. But contempt is a different register. Contempt says: I have written this person out of the category of people who deserve understanding.

Whoever isn't in the room today will be in the room eventually. And then they will be talked about the same way.

The way someone narrates their past is a very reliable preview of how they will one day narrate you.

One to reflect on: who do you become in the stories that person tells about others?

Full framework is in the link in my bio.
